articles.title_orig: Type 004: China’s Fourth Carrier May Outgrow the Ford Class
articles.title_zh: Type 004: China’s Fourth Carrier May Outgrow the Ford Class
articles.content_orig:
by Fortuné Leroy | Nov 21, 2026 | Militärische Luftfahrt , Nachricht | 0 comments
In a dry dock at Dalian, the same one that built China’s first two aircraft carriers, a hull is growing that may end up as long as America’s newest supercarriers. Satellite images taken on 4 September 2026 show the bulbous bow taking shape. Once it is finished, Janes estimates, the ship will be 336 to 339 metres long, marginally longer than USS Gerald R. Ford. Beijing has not given the carrier a name, released a single figure or even confirmed what it is.
Analysts call it the Type 004. It will be China’s fourth carrier, and the first that looks built to match America’s supercarriers rather than chase them.
The work has been visible from orbit since early 2025, when prefabricated modules appeared at Dalian. Keel blocks followed in mid-2025, and by May 2026 imagery showed something no Chinese carrier had had before: two internal compartments, each about 15 by 15 metres, the size and layout analysts would expect for a pair of reactors. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which has tracked the hull month by month, measured it at about 322 metres from the unfinished bow to the stern in October, with a beam of about 46 metres.
Nuclear power would give the PLA Navy a carrier that can stay at sea for long periods without refuelling and generate the electricity needed for electromagnetic catapults. CSIS rates nuclear propulsion as likely, but it has never been confirmed, and the only other evidence is a land-based prototype naval reactor in Sichuan reported by the Associated Press in 2024.
China’s first two carriers, Liaoning and Shandong, launch their J-15 fighters off a ski-jump bow, which limits how heavy the aircraft can be. Fujian, commissioned at Sanya on 5 November 2025 with Xi Jinping in attendance, was the leap: about 80,000 tonnes, conventionally powered, with three electromagnetic catapults, the technology the US Navy introduced with the Ford in 2017. Her air wing includes the catapult-launched J-15T, the stealthy J-35 and the KJ-600 early-warning aircraft.
Fujian one year after commissioning. Video: CCTV Video News Agency.
The Type 004 is expected to go further. Analysts expect electromagnetic catapults again, possibly four, and a bigger air wing; Lyle Goldstein of Defense Priorities has estimated 75 to 90 aircraft, against roughly 50 to 60 on Fujian. China is also experimenting with drones at sea: in November 2026 the new amphibious assault ship Sichuan launched and recovered a GJ-21 stealth drone with its own electromagnetic catapult.
The United States still operates 11 nuclear-powered carriers, and the second Ford-class ship, John F. Kennedy, reached preliminary acceptance in September 2026, with full delivery due in March 2027. Its first F-35C landing came on 13 October. But the Pentagon’s latest report on China’s military expects the gap in numbers to keep narrowing.
In Washington, meanwhile, the argument is about going backwards. An August White House memo ordered a plan to fit the future USS Doris Miller with steam catapults instead of electromagnetic ones. On 17 November 2026, Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told the Navy’s leadership in a hearing that “returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that.”
Flight operations aboard USS Gerald R. Ford. Video: US Navy.
Almost everything about the Type 004 is still an estimate: its final length, its displacement, its power plant and the number of catapults. China has confirmed none of it. If it follows Fujian’s pattern, the hull could float out of the dock in 2027, and the carrier could join the fleet some years after that. What the satellites already make clear is the ambition: a Chinese carrier built in the same weight class as the American ones.

Ford command history; Associated Press (2024).

articles.title_orig: Cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad hit by drones, Finland tightens security
articles.title_zh: Cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad hit by drones, Finland tightens security
articles.content_orig:
Rescue efforts are under way in the Gulf of Finland after a Russian cargo ship was hit by drones close to Russia’s maritime border.
The ship, the Sparta II, is on fire and has now drifted into Finnish territorial waters, authorities say.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.
A photograph taken by a Border Guard patrol plane shows flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland temporarily instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
Finland’s Border Guard said the vessel is known to have links to the Russian armed forces.
According to the Border Guard, the crew of the Sparta II have not been forced to abandon ship, and there has been no environmental damage so far from the drone attack, while the vessel is in the open sea off the southern coastal town of Loviisa.
“The Border Guard is preparing to evacuate people and assist in firefighting operations,” Finnish authorities said.
It is not clear who was behind the attack, but Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the damage had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of Saint Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said air and sea traffic restrictions had been put in place as a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about striking in the area afterwards.

articles.title_orig: Skip the junk: What retail experts say is actually worth buying on Black Friday
articles.title_zh: Skip the junk: What retail experts say is actually worth buying on Black Friday
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Dean Ornish, Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Alan Cohen
When people tell Dr. Dean Ornish they want to live longer, he asks them why. Maybe they want to dance at their kid’s wedding, they say, or finally write the book they’ve been thinking about for years. Whatever their answer, it gives them something to work toward and can make changing a habit today feel worth the effort.
Knowing what you want to stay healthy enough to do can shape the questions you ask at a doctor’s visit. It can also help you make sense of options like biological-age tests, peptides, and new uses for weight-loss drugs. At a TIME100 Talks panel in New York on Thursday titled “The Future of Men’s Health: From Reactive Treatment to Personalized Prevention,” three experts discussed how those goals can guide decisions about care.
What does that look like when a patient comes in with a specific complaint? TIME senior health correspondent Alice Park, who moderated the panel, asked how doctors could use that visit to talk about prevention. Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer of Hims—which sponsored the event—said the language doctors use often keeps the conversation focused on what’s wrong.
“We have terms like ‘history of present illness,’ ‘chief complaint,’ ‘problem list,’” Vinjamoori said. He suggested asking patients early in the visit what they hope to get out of their care. Their answer can help doctors figure out which preventive steps are worth talking through, he added.
To get ahead of age-related health problems, it would help to know when someone is aging faster than expected. Park asked Alan Cohen, who chairs biological complexity and healthy longevity at Columbia University, how researchers make that distinction. Even defining aging is tricky, he said. In a survey he helped lead , scientists who study aging disagreed on what it is, when it begins, and whether it can be measured.
“I think health is actually an easier target to measure than aging,” Cohen said. A biological-age test can be good at estimating how old you are, he explained, while leaving some of the questions that matter most in daily life unanswered. “Are you able to be and do the things that matter to you?” he asked. A clinician might measure how well someone walks, he said. He’d also want to know whether that person can get to the store.
Park asked about peptides, which some people are trying on their own in hopes of improving their health. “This is not a one size fits all—there’s not a peptide or compound that everyone here should be on. Everyone’s going to have their own unique answer here. I think individualization is the name of the game, ” Vinjamoori said. “My advice, first and foremost is to work with someone on your journey, right? As much excitement as you might have to dive in on your own.”
He suggested talking with a clinician about peptides, which he noted is a service that Hims & Hers is now offering .
He also cautioned against purchasing products sold as “research use only,” and emphasized the importance of vetted suppliers. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has flagged potential safety risks with compounded BPC-157, for example, saying it has too little information to determine whether it could harm people.
The evidence is stronger for some peptides than for others. Ornish, founder and president of the Preventive Medicine Research Institute, said he sees GLP-1 drugs as a possible “jumpstart” that can help people feel well enough to make changes they can stick with. He pointed to a large clinical trial that enrolled adults with established cardiovascular disease and a BMI in the overweight or obesity range. The trial excluded people with diabetes. Compared with a placebo, those taking semaglutide experienced a lowered relative risk of heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death.
When Park asked where someone who feels overwhelmed by health advice should start, Ornish suggested picking something you can do even on a busy day. “If I don’t have time to meditate for an hour, do it for a minute,” he said. If a half-hour walk is out of reach, he suggested walking around the room while you’re on the phone. “I think the consistency is more important than anything else.”
TIME100 Talk: The Future of Men's Health: From Personalized Treatment to Reactive Care was presented by Hims.
The original version of this story misstated Dr. Anant Vinjamoori's title. He is the chief medical officer of Hims, not the chief medical officer of Hims & Hers.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title_orig: China Sends Missile-Carrying Bomber Toward Manila, Turns Back Just 170 Kilometers From Capital
articles.title_zh: China Sends Missile-Carrying Bomber Toward Manila, Turns Back Just 170 Kilometers From Capital
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese H-6 bomber capable of carrying long-range cruise missiles approached the Philippine capital, Manila, before turning back approximately 170 kilometers (106 miles) from the city, raising speculation that the aircraft may have been rehearsing a missile strike.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on November 21, the Chinese military aircraft was briefly detected on the public flight-tracking platform ADS-B Exchange while operating over the South China Sea, between the disputed Scarborough Shoal and the Philippine island of Luzon.
Defense journalist Mike Yeo shared a screenshot of the aircraft’s flight path, noting that the bomber “popped up for a minute” on the tracking platform.
The aircraft was identified on the service as a Tupolev Tu-16, the Soviet-designed bomber that served as the basis for China’s modern H-6 family. Flight data indicated that it was operating at approximately 8,000 meters (26,450 feet), without a publicly displayed call sign.
The recorded route showed the bomber approaching from the northwest before turning east toward the Philippine coast. It then performed a tight loop and returned along its original route.
An X user known as Dianbo, who follows Chinese military developments, claimed the aircraft turned approximately 170 kilometers from Manila, suggesting the maneuver could have simulated the launch of an AKD-63B air-to-surface missile.
The missile reportedly has a range of approximately 240 kilometers (149 miles), placing Manila within its theoretical striking distance from the bomber’s reported turning point.
The flight took place near Scarborough Shoal, a disputed reef in the South China Sea claimed by both China and the Philippines. The area has become a recurring location for Chinese military aviation and naval operations.
China operates approximately 219 H-6-family bombers, according to Defence Blog. The aircraft originated from the Soviet Tu-16 design but has undergone extensive modernization, including upgraded engines, expanded weapons capabilities, and aerial refueling equipment on certain variants.
The Philippines is a US treaty ally, and its northern military facilities could become strategically important in a potential Taiwan conflict. That makes Chinese military pressure on the Philippines relevant not only to the South China Sea dispute but also to the wider US-China military balance in the region.
Earlier, in April 2026, China deployed two H-6 anti-ship bombers escorted by J-16 fighter jets over Scarborough Shoal during US-Philippine military exercises involving approximately 17,000 personnel.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
Paul Smith, chief commercial officer of Anthropic, center left, and Krishna Rao, chief financial officer of Anthropic, center right, alongside others react during the closing bell ceremony for the Anthropic IPO at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

articles.title_orig: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
articles.title_zh: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
articles.content_orig:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.
Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before in the 24 years countries have been meeting.
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas .
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.

articles.title_orig: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.title_zh: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.content_orig:
The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.
U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.
Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites , bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.
It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.
The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.
A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.
"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.
The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.
"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."
There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.
A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.
American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.
Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)
Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.
American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.
"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."
Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.
On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.
First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.
And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.
"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."
Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites , respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.
American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.
Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.
Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.
United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options , which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.
There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.
"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."
Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.
Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.
British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.
Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways , Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats .
"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

articles.title_orig: Strait of Hormuz attacks have increased to highest level since Iran war began - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Strait of Hormuz attacks have increased to highest level since Iran war began - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The attacks could complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing.
Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the war between the U.S., Israel and Iran began in late February , according to data compiled by maritime organizations.
The attacks appear to be a bid to complicate U.S.-led efforts to keep oil flowing through the economically crucial Strait of Hormuz despite an Iranian-declared blockade, experts told ABC News.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 31 attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October, and about 19 in November, as of Nov. 18.
Previously, a total of 53 incidents had been reported to the UKMTO between March and September of this year, averaging 10 to 15 incidents total across both Strait of Hormuz and surrounding gulfs in previous months.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a United Nations agency, has slightly more conservative numbers, with 34 attacks confirmed in and around the Strait of Hormuz in October and November so far.
This too, is still a marked increase from previous numbers the IMO had collected, which number roughly 50 in and around the Strait of Hormuz between March and September. The IMO has tallied 138 attacks on vessels in total across the Middle East since the war began.
The positions of attacked tankers reported to the UKMTO indicate that most attacked vessels were in the very southern portion of the Strait of Hormuz, staying close to the Omani coastline, according to the maritime group's data.
"Iran's objective remains to keep the Omani route, which is described as a U.S.-facilitated route, a very high-risk passage and to keep the energy recovery inconsistent," Noam Raydan, senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told ABC News.
"Washington and its regional partners have found ways to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told ABC News. "Tehran now seems determined to make these arrangements more costly and less reliable."
The workaround developed by the U.S. involves "ship-to-ship" (STS) transfers in which smaller tankers cross the strait with tracking systems switched off, and transfer cargos to larger tankers once safely on the other side, Sina Toossi, senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, told ABC News.
Iran is now responding in "a cycle of adaptation and counter-adaptation," he said.
"Tehran has escalated its attacks to make the STS system more dangerous, costly, and ultimately unviable. Iran's broader objective is to demonstrate that normal oil exports cannot continue while the US maintains its blockade of Iran, and to generate enough economic pressure to force Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict," Toossi said.
The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade, stopping Iranian and Iran-linked ships from going in and out of the Gulf of Oman, starting April 13, with a brief pause from June 18 to July 13.
Strikes have not been limited to ships. On Nov. 8, Iran attacked the Omani island of Didamar in the strait itself, according to satellite images and video verified by ABC News.
The island hosts radar and satellite communications technology. Iranian state media said Iran had struck what it described as "enemy navigation aid systems." Oman, a U.S. partner, did not comment on the attack.
Strikes have also not been isolated to ships actively crossing the strait. ABC News has verified at least one incident in which a ship was attacked by a drone appearing to belong to Iran, despite not making any attempt to cross the strait.
In early October, the Panama-flagged supertanker Gem No. 2 had been idle off the coast of the United Arab Emirates in the Persian Gulf, outside the Strait of Hormuz, for nearly five months.
It was fully loaded with a cargo of two million barrels of Saudi crude oil, per maritime intelligence company Kpler, and was one of the hundreds of ships the International Maritime Organization estimates is stuck in the Persian Gulf since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
Two crew members who were on board Gem No. 2 say the ship never attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and that it was attacked by one drone on Oct. 9 and then at least three others on Oct. 10, the latter attack sparking a massive fire and forcing the ship's evacuation, according to videos filmed by the crew obtained and verified by ABC News.
Hours after the vessel was struck for a second time and evacuated, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in an online post that the vessel had struck a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route.
Satellite images taken in the days after it was abandoned confirm Gem No. 2's position off the coast of the UAE, well outside the Strait of Hormuz.
ABC News showed images taken by the crew of the wreckage of the drone that struck the ship on Oct. 9 to Fabian Hinz, a researcher who studies drone warfare. Hinz said the wreckage in the images belongs to a jet-powered Hadid-110, built by Iran. Iran continues to say the ship hit a mine.
Azizi, the ICG's Iran analyst, suggested that "large oil tankers seem to be receiving particular attention, whether they are moving through the strait or operating elsewhere in the Persian Gulf."
"One possible explanation is that Tehran wants to discourage the use of supertankers and prevent the development of alternative shipping arrangements that could make the blockade less effective," he said.
It's not clear why Gem No. 2 was allegedly targeted, but the vessel would have been an easy target, according to Samir Madani, co-founder of TankerTrackers.c o m . Madani told ABC News he noticed Gem No. 2 before the attack because the tanker's location transmission services were turned on, revealing its location publicly.
Both Azizi and Toossi describe Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz as having "strategic logic."
"Ultimately, the objective goes beyond disrupting oil exports. Iran is trying to demonstrate that the United States cannot guarantee maritime security in the Persian Gulf despite its overwhelming naval superiority," Azizi told ABC News.
Toossi added that this strategy will have consequences far beyond the strait.
"The danger is that this escalating contest will produce a much wider disruption of regional shipping and energy infrastructure, with even greater consequences for the global economy," he said.

articles.title_zh: Shaking reported in Australia after magnitude 6.8 earthquake rocks Timor-Leste, Pacific Ring of Fire
articles.content_orig:
While you may think quakes are a western US problem, some of the largest temblors in US history have happened in the East.
DILI, TIMOR-LESTE — A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck the Banda Sea about 65 miles northeast of Timor-Leste in Southeast Asia just after 4:30 a.m. ET (6:30 p.m. local time), according to the USGS.
MAGNITUDE 4.2 EARTHQUAKE SHAKES LOS ANGELES FOLLOWING FLURRY OF SEISMIC ACTIVITY ACROSS CENTRAL CALIFORNIA
(FOX Weather / FOX Weather)
The Southeast Asian nation shares the island of Timor with Indonesia, north of Australia .
The quake's epicenter was nearly 90 miles below the surface but was felt in the capital of Dili, as well as Darwin, Australia, some 400 miles to the southeast.
An aerial image shows the view of the city in Dili, East Timor on September 12, 2024.
((Photo by Yasuyoshi CHIBA / AFP) (Photo by YASUYOSHI CHIBA/AFP via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.
Timor-Leste sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a 25,000-mile belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean , where about 90% of the world's earthquakes occur.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
articles.content_orig:
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace , and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5 , each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge , which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.
Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.
He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.
“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.
“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”
Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.
“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”
He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.
On the same day, Denmark took action on a separate front. It announced that it was expelling Russia’s defence attache after Danish intelligence concluded that Moscow had orchestrated a plot to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner during a concert near Copenhagen.

articles.title_orig: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
articles.title_zh: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
articles.content_orig:
Gun-toting robots trotting down a dark alley. The blaze of a helicopter-launched rocket. A gang boss’s mansion crumbling in the sunshine.
Thousands of Salvadoran troops landed in Haiti last month to combat gangs overrunning the Caribbean nation. While it’s too early to tell if they’re succeeding, the personal involvement of popular Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has stirred rare hope on the island – and avid interest across Latin America.
What’s the difference between the newly arrived Salvadorans and all the other fighting forces in Haiti’s crowded security landscape? “They’re really good at making videos,” one local security source said.
Most of what we know about the Salvadoran force has come in glimpses from Bukele’s social media accounts. The deal governing their presence has not been made public, but the 45-year-old president is effectively drumming up support with promises in Creole to root out the gangs as he has done in El Salvador, combined with explosive footage and online banter.
“For the first time, I felt like someone had listened to me,” said Sophia Fecu, describing the moment she saw a video posted by Bukele that showed helicopters attacking gang leader Lanmo Sanjou’s house on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince. “I felt like my voice had finally been heard.”
Days earlier, Fecu, a Haitian entrepreneur and writer, had posted a picture of the notorious gang clubhouse on X and tagged Bukele. “I just felt that it wasn’t right for these criminals to be living so comfortably while the rest of the population was forced to flee their homes and communities,” she said from the US, where she now lives. “I honestly didn’t expect him to respond.”
But he did. Bukele answered on X asking for the location of the house, sparking a flurry of responses. Three days later, he posted an update : Video of helicopters blasting apart the building’s blue-tiled facade, shadowy figures of suspected gang members fleeing the compound on foot.
Bukele adds a wildcard to Haiti’s fractured security landscape
It’s hard to imagine other forces in Haiti crowdsourcing coordinates for a well-known gang headquarters. But Haitian police, a secretive task force involving a private military contractor led by Erik Prince , and the multinational Gang Suppression Force have been busy, too: Police announced on Thursday that they had killed 34 gang members in a major operation in the Port-au-Prince neighborhood of Martissant. The GSF, still building its force, said its operations are entering a “new phase” of pressure and is also posting more videos of soldiers at work. But no one boasts the same reach as Bukele.
Some friction was inevitable. Security sources in Haiti complain about a lack of cooperation and credit-sharing with the Salvadorans and point out that fighting videos don’t show the difficult reality of working in Haiti, like finding parts to repair helicopters damaged by gang fire.
Last week, Salvadoran troops reportedly fired perilously close to GSF troops. On another occasion, they sparked tensions after trying to enter a GSF outpost without notice, sources said. On Friday, two soldiers died and two others were wounded in an incident handling explosive material , according to the Salvadoran army.
Still, there is hope for a deeper eventual collaboration once the new force finds its footing. And Bukele will need it. He has raised expectations in an exhausted nation, and now he must deliver. His troops are far from home and facing a gang alliance that knows the terrain better, can replace fallen soldiers with forced conscripts, and shares information and resources across Port-au-Prince.
Can hired mercenaries succeed where others have failed?
“Imagine if the police, task force, GSF and Salvadorans were all working together, with their combined ground and air forces — that would be amazing,” a security source said wistfully.

articles.title_orig: Walmart shoppers stocked up on emergency supplies after series of tech outages: report
articles.title_zh: Walmart shoppers stocked up on emergency supplies after series of tech outages: report
articles.content_orig:
Walmart said U.S. shoppers stocked up on bottled water, propane and camping gear amid panic buying after a string of recent technology outages.
Walmart shoppers were stocking up on numerous emergency supplies following a series of technology outages that disrupted day-to-day activities and alarmed Americans across the country.
Shoppers loaded their carts with propane, bottled water and camping gear, a Walmart spokesperson told Reuters.
"We have seen a small amount of that. Certainly, categories like jug bottled water or propane are selling at higher comps with that concern, but it’s really relatively small to our overall business. It’s worth noting that oftentimes when we see that, it’s a pull forward of future demand," Walmart's Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey told Yahoo Finance.
The retailer also raised its annual sales and profit forecasts on Thursday, anticipating growth in its delivery and membership as it prepares for the holiday shopping season.
COSTCO SEES PANIC BUYING SURGE AFTER TECH OUTAGES, REPORT SAYS
Walmart shoppers were stocking up on numerous emergency supplies following a series of technology outages. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Walmart is the largest retailer to report the uptick in emergency supply purchases, but other companies said they experienced similar sales in response to the outages.
Costco and Tractor Supply are among the other retailers to see an increase in demand amid a wave of apparent panic buying.
Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger said that the string of technology disruptions led to a sudden surge in emergency preparedness shopping at Costco.
About 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators Costco offers on its website were completely sold out as of Sunday night, according to a note released by Mizuho Securities on Monday.
Among the wiped-out inventory were massive whole-home backup systems priced as high as nearly $7,000.
Walmart shoppers stocked up on propane, bottled water and camping gear. (REUTERS/Mike Blake / Reuters)
"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights , and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at [Costco]," Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger said in the note.
The buying spree has helped put Costco on pace for rare double-digit U.S. sales growth this month, marking a level not seen since mid-2022.
Alongside backup generators, shoppers are also aggressively "pantry-loading" on bulk essentials ahead of the holiday season , the report said.
WALMART RAISES FULL-YEAR OUTLOOK AS WEALTHIER SHOPPERS FUEL SALES GROWTH
Costco and Tractor Supply are among the other retailers to see an increase in demand for emergency supplies. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images)

Bellinger raised his price target on Costco shares from $1,100 to $1,150 on the back of the heightened demand.
Meanwhile, Tractor Supply said sales of products like generators, liquid storage tanks and propane accessories are trending higher this year, the company told Bloomberg News. For the first time, shoppers are buying these products at a higher rate than across other product groups.
This comes shortly after a series of disruptions hit the U.S. within days, including a Microsoft outage, a nationwide ground stop caused by an air traffic control failure, a United Airlines technology breakdown and software problems that disrupted some JPMorgan Chase services.

articles.title_orig: The Danger of Jensen Huang’s Handshake Deals at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: The Danger of Jensen Huang’s Handshake Deals at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
The day before Colette Kress led her first earnings call as Nvidia's interim CEO, she did not want to talk about her predecessor, Jensen Huang .
"This is a new era for Nvidia," she told employees in an internal meeting on Monday, according to a person present, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. When someone brought up Huang, Kress quickly changed the subject, according to the person.
On Wednesday, Kress addressed the whole company at the first Nvidia all-hands meeting since the public chaos over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and other reported relationships. And while Kress will be tasked with filling the leadership vacuum created by Huang's departure, she is also tamping down public calls to bring him back.
Huang himself weighed in with his first public statement Tuesday saying he would be "honored" to return to Nvidia.
Kress, who has served as the company's CFO since 2013, must steady employees and convince customers and investors that Nvidia can execute on its ambitious targets without the man who made them.
At Wednesday's meeting with staffers, Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones as well as Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's hyperscale and high performance computing business, according to an attendee.
Kress' message was, "Let's move forward," said the person, who asked not to be named because the event was private.
Nvidia's leaders have made clear that the board does not plan to bring Huang back.
"The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen," Kress said in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday. "We want to grow in terms of everything that we need to do with our employees, our customers, our shareholders, and that is where we are going to focus moving forward."
Jones echoed the sentiment on Tuesday's earnings call. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said in opening remarks.
Nvidia declined to comment for this story.
Kress stressed on the earnings call that the company was focused on the workers who remain, who she said are "committed to doing their life's work at Nvidia." The company also reported better-than-expected earnings and seemed to calm investors' nerves , at least for the moment.
Some employees are telling a different story. Support for Huang's return is growing inside Nvidia, sources tell CNBC. An online petition circulating since the weekend has nearly 200,000 signatures, with more than 10,000 of them claiming to be current Nvidia employees. Nvidia currently has roughly 42,000 employees.
Outside Nvidia, Huang's reinstatement has been called for by at least two major investors and tech heavyweights such as Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang return as CEO.
Several employees posted on X over the last few days, voicing support for Huang and calling for his return. One robotics engineer said the founder's departure led to his own decision to leave.
Another senior Nvidia employee, Nader Khalil, sent a letter to the company's board and top executives warning that failing to reinstate Huang could lead to a loss of "irreplaceable talent," according to The Wall Street Journal.
Huang was known for his deep day-to-day involvement in his company's operations, often responding directly to engineers and chiming in personally on technical projects.
Engineering employees, in particular, were "extremely devoted to him, almost like a demigod," according to a former Nvidia employee who was at the company for more than 15 years and spoke to CNBC on condition of anonymity.
Wednesday's all-hands is a standard meeting: Nvidia traditionally holds one on the morning after each quarterly earnings call, according to the former employee.
Still, the meeting is unlike anything the company has experienced. Employees told CNBC that they plan to share their grievances at the all-hands, though it wasn't clear ahead of time if they would be allowed to ask questions.
Huang took time to address employee questions during previous post-earnings all-hands meetings, the former Nvidia employee told CNBC, adding that Kress is "eager to demonstrate there's a new sheriff in town."
Kress ended Tuesday's earnings call with an upbeat message: "Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We've got this."
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI Hits 60 FPS and Above on Xbox Series X Through a Quick Resume Glitch, but Gameplay Runs at Double Speed
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI Hits 60 FPS and Above on Xbox Series X Through a Quick Resume Glitch, but Gameplay Runs at Double Speed
articles.content_orig:
In true Rockstar Games tradition, Grand Theft Auto VI launched with a 30 FPS target on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S due to technical reasons, as even the PlayStation 5 Pro's CPU cannot handle the game's complex simulation at 60 FPS . However, besides using some PC tools to bring the framerate of streamed console gameplay up to 60 FPS or higher, there's a way to enjoy the latest entry in the series at an unlocked framerate on Xbox Series X via a glitch, though with some catches.
The Grand Theft Auto VI FPS unlock glitch was discovered by Reddit user Meowwie64 , who detailed the entire process on the GTA6unmoderated subreddit :
"I somehow unlocked my framerate on GTA VI via a weird glitch within the Xbox's Quick Resume Feature that allows GTA VI to run at an unlocked framerate ."
1. An Xbox Series X (Maybe does work on Series S too can't test it myself, though)
3. Grand Theft Auto VI (on Game Version 01.002.001; this glitch may still work on later versions not sure)
1. Put your Xbox display settings to 60Hz
3. Wait until you see the 6 Stars in the Intro
4. Change your display settings back to 120Hz
5. Cold Boot another game on your console via the Xbox Guide (The Xbox button) and without quitting GTA VI
7. Now enjoy GTA VI at an unlocked framerate"
As mentioned above, there are some catches. As the game speed is tied to animation, something that was rather common in past generations, Grand Theft Auto VI essentially speeds up when the framerate goes beyond the 30 FPS lock. However, looking at the footage shared by the user, cutscenes do work well even at 60+ FPS.
Given that Grand Theft Auto VI can run at 60 FPS or higher on Xbox Series X , one can only wonder why Rockstar Games still targets 30 FPS on all systems. Although we can only speculate at this point, it's likely related to overall performance stability. As the framerate often dips below 30 FPS even on the PlayStation 5 Pro , it's likely that a 60 FPS target or an unlocked framerate would have produced jarring performance swings, resulting in anything but an enjoyable experience.
About the author : Francesco De Meo has been covering video games and technology since 2012, starting his career at small outlets like Gamersyndrome and GeekSnack. 

After joining the Wccftech gaming section in 2015, he quickly expanded his video gaming coverage with in-depth reporting, interviews with iconic industry figures such as Grasshopper Manufacture founder and No More Heroes creator Goichi "Suda51" Suda, Resident Evil series creator Shinji Mikami, Team NINJA's president and Nioh series director Fumihiko Yasuda, and Silent Hill creator Keiichiro Toyama, reviews and on-the-ground coverage of major industry events such as Gamescom and E3.

When he's not reporting or reviewing, Francesco can be found playing the genres he loves most, spending time with his six cats, reading, writing music, playing guitar and drumming for his progressive rock band.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.title_zh: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.content_orig:
JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group , on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah , which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars in Jurf al-Sakhar.
The hardline Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations, which have led to arrests that prompted fears of an armed response . The group is among those that have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
A convoy of vehicles flying Iraqi flags headed into Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday and soldiers took up positions in the center after senior security officials told a press conference that government forces would protect the town.
Members of the Kataib Hezbollah group stood near their group’s flags.
“From Jurf al-Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of Iraq, confronting corruption and weapons beyond state control,” Zaidi told government troops who entered the town, speaking from a military operations center in Baghdad.
“Our decision is firm: No weapons outside state authority, no weapons but Iraq‘s, no decisions but Iraq‘s, and no flag shall fly higher than the Iraqi flag.”
Under the arrangement, brokered by Shi’ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq , a major oil producer and ally of both the US and Iran.
“God willing, things will be safe and secure with the presence of the security forces,” said resident Mohamed Ali.
The deal will include the opening of a security headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar on Saturday to oversee the handover. Iraq‘s energy police have begun securing an oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, the state news agency reported.
“Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi Armed Forces prove that they are the nation’s shield, safety valve, and the guardian ensuring security stability for the Iraqi people,” Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, told the press conference.
Reflecting the sensitivity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political figures said Esmail Qaani , commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah.
So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad.
Any direct confrontation with Iran’s heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.
After one of Zaidi’s predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on those armed groups five years ago, the prime minister’s Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.
US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February.
Kataib Hezbollah and other militias, all of whom report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, have refused to hand over their weapons to the state.
Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq , the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organisations supported by Iran.
Kataib Hezbollah quickly developed a reputation for deadly attacks against military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counterinsurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs.
Since the 2003 US-led invasion toppled Iran’s arch-enemy, longtime Sunni leader Saddam Hussein, Tehran has steadily expanded its influence in Iraq through close ties with heavily armed Shi’ite militias and political parties.
Iraqi security officials say the militias’ arsenals include assault rifles, machineguns, anti-tank guided missiles , mortars, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missile capabilities.
Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though Kataib denies this and says it is dedicated to security .
Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.
It forms several battalions in Iraq‘s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognized as an official security force.
Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF. While it is technically under the command of Iraq‘s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command.

articles.title_orig: Zelda's Ocarina Remake Is One Of Metacritic's Highest-Rated Games In 2026, According To User Scores
articles.title_zh: Zelda's Ocarina Remake Is One Of Metacritic's Highest-Rated Games In 2026, According To User Scores
articles.content_orig:
It's been a huge year for the games industry with all sorts of heavy-hitters releasing over the past few months, and as we look towards the end of 2026, we're now checking in on Metacritic's highest-rated games of the year based on the user score .
While Grand Theft Auto 6 may have officially surpassed Ocarina's Remake as the highest-rated game of 2026 on the review aggregate website (and also matched the original N64 hit as the highest-rated critic Metascore of all time ), it seems the classic outing on Switch 2 has won players' hearts worldwide.
According to the latest update from the site, Ocarina's Remake is currently sitting in the top highest-rated games (above 90), based on user score (it's on 9.2/10 at the time of writing). It's in good company with other games like Resident Evil Requiem and Splatoon Raiders .
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Obviously, there are all sorts of different factors in play here when it comes to user scores (and the system in place isn't necessarily perfect). For example, Ocarina's Remake has over 25,000 user reviews , whereas other titles may have around 100 reviews. Keep in mind, user scores are also subject to change over time.
And if you're wondering how GTA 6 has been received by players, it's currently sitting on a user score of 5.5/10 after more than 30,000 user reviews . Even with supposed review bombings , it might take some time before it wins over some players. Despite top marks from critics, this new entry in the GTA universe appears to have divided the fanbase in its opening week.
As attention shifts towards the end-of-year game awards, both Ocarina and GTA 6 have already been nominated for multiple industry awards.

articles.title_orig: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.title_zh: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.
