articles.title_orig: Google Is Killing the Nest App. Here’s What Comes Next
articles.title_zh: Google Is Killing the Nest App. Here’s What Comes Next
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Google Home is replacing Nest and bringing new devices.
If you’re a Nest smart home user, a major change is coming in early 2027 that will affect how you manage your smart home. Google has officially confirmed to CNET via email that both the Nest app and Google Assistant are being sunset, and current users will lose access to both next year.
All Nest devices will lose Nest app support in favor of the Google Home app, and the Nest app will be retired on Jan. 25, 2027. Google Assistant will be removed from home devices on Aug. 2, 2027, with all support moving to the Gemini for Home voice assistant.
The change is part of Google’s effort to consolidate its various apps and devices into a single app and voice experience. In a statement sent to CNET, Google confirmed that “every device supported today works with these updated experiences.”
Nest Thermostats should all seamlessly port over to Google Home.
Google has confirmed that Google Home will support all your Nest devices, including thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke detectors and locks. Existing schedules and settings should transfer over automatically, which is often a hassle when you switch between apps and devices. You should also be able to pair your Nest devices with any Works with Google Home and Matter smart home devices, as well as Google Home speakers and smart displays and TV streamers, all with the same app.
As part of the switchover, you should be able to access Nest devices on various platforms outside of the mobile app. It’ll support iOS and Android widgets, the Home Panel on Android, smart displays, speakers and the Google Home web page. That includes being able to check live camera views, adjust your thermostat and lock your front door, right from a TV or smartwatch.
Google Assistant may be leaving, but Google is releasing newer, more powerful devices.
Google says that, in addition to devices automatically appearing in the Favorites tab in the Google Home app, you should be able to see camera views faster and access the most-used controls the moment you open the app. Part of the goal is to give users the latest security protections and cyber defenses, as well as Google Account security, privacy controls and threat protections –- all things that seem extra relevant these days as major companies across the US seem to be experiencing outages .
However, to continue controlling and receiving notifications from your Nest devices remotely, you will need to switch to the Google Home app or home.google.com if you prefer to control them via a web browser.
You can change Google voice assistant voices, but not the wake words.
On Aug. 2, 2027, Gemini for Home voice assistant will fully replace Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays. The switch to Gemini makes a lot of sense if you’ve used Google Assistant at all. Assistant is very much an older voice assistant, lacking the smarter follow-ups and natural-language capabilities that make Gemini more useful. With Gemini, you should get answers to more complex questions, and you can speak more naturally without barking commands, letting it handle conversation context and remember multiple interactions.
Getting ready for Google Home is easy, though Google has an entire Nest App Transition Support Hub if you need step-by-step instructions to walk you through everything that’s needed.
For most people, it should be a simple matter of downloading the Google Home app. Naturally, a Google Account is required, but as mentioned, your Nest devices, including the cameras and video history, will automatically transfer from the Nest app starting on Jan. 25, 2027.
Gemini’s Google Home integrations are useful, but command options can include some risks.
The other thing you may have to do is download any custom video clips you’ve created on home.nest.com . Manually saved clips won’t transfer to the Google Home app along with your video history. To make sure these are backed up, you’ll want to visit home.nest.com before Jan. 25, 2027, and use the Download All button to save clips you want to keep.
The final deadline to migrate your Nest account to a Google account before the company starts data deletions March 25, 2027.
Google says Nest devices, including cameras and video history, will automatically transfer from the Nest app to the Google Home app. Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions should also automatically switch to Google Home Premium so that coverage continues without interruption. Google Home Premium is replacing Nest Aware (1st Gen), and users will receive an email closer to the transfer date detailing your subscription information.
Google’s smart displays should all work perfectly with the various Nest devices.
Gemini for Home is already available in many countries and languages. Google announced earlier that it’s expanding to more regions over the coming months. Users in a supported region can upgrade to Gemini Home right now.
On your phone, open the latest version of the Google Home app, tap your profile icon in the top right to open Home Settings, then tap “Get Started” on the “Set up Gemini for Home” banner. On your computer, just visit home.google.com/gemini .

articles.title_orig: The Fear Gauge Hit 40. This Is What the Market Is Worried About.
articles.title_zh: The Fear Gauge Hit 40. This Is What the Market Is Worried About.
articles.content_orig:
There's a bull market... in fear.
Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide tech outages to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering, traders on Tuesday piled into protective put options on the S&P 500 Index at a rate that suggests fear beyond just an AI-specific correction. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged nearly 5 points to a high of 27.7 at the worst of Tuesday's selling and the ratio of put to call volumes on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) hit 1.5, the highest since the first week of April, according to Barchart data. The 'VIX' was last still hovering above 26. With the VIX climbing four days in a row, the volatility gauge hasn't traded under 16 since Oct. 16, arguably trending higher as the S&P 500 slips below this month's lows, trading under 7,300 for the lowest price for the benchmark equity gauge since June. Cboe's three-month volatility gauge, VIX3M, briefly touched the highest since April.
While Nvidia earnings are contributing to the uncertainty – the stock's options currently imply more than a 7% move after its report, the biggest in almost two years – volatility in the S&P 500 jumped more than in the Nasdaq 100 Tuesday, pointing to a more widespread fear among investors. "SPX vol is expanding faster than NDX vol, as SPX vol is coming from a lower base," Eric Metz, CIO, SpiderRock Advisors for BlackRock, said via email. "Today, the market is pricing acute near-term stress in large-caps broadly, but tech-specific fear is still notable. Even within the technology cohort, Tuesday's laggards took on a different tone. Software stocks declined the most ahead of Anthropic's IPO, with options volume on the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) surging to almost four times the 30-day average, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Salesforce was hardest hit, with put contracts outpacing calls on twice the average options volume. "There's a lot of reasons to be risk-off," said Noel Smith, co-CIO of Kai Asset Management. "This is a market-wide phenomenon today that's not just AI stocks." To be sure, bulls weren't totally absent from the session, with the Nasdaq 100 Index holding its November low and VIX still under its Nov. 5 high of 28.4. "While vol is now at a relatively elevated level, we have not seen much fear in the options market," said VolSignals' Matthew Nadel, citing fixed-strike volatility in S&P 500 options, which measures volatility changes across specific options strikes. "We have seen a pretty decent move higher in SPX fixed strike vol, however the move up in vol has been mostly orderly."

articles.title_orig: AI tech rout prompts US investors to rush into value stocks
articles.title_zh: AI tech rout prompts US investors to rush into value stocks
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over.
The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com , which tracks private-company shares.
As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million.
“What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”
Anthropic valued at $1.76 trillion after first day of trading
It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday.
But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024.
As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”
SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000.
Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.)
And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth.
A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years.
The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
CNN’s Samantha Delouya contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: US tech stocks plunge into bear market in worst week since Covid-19 crisis
articles.title_zh: US tech stocks plunge into bear market in worst week since Covid-19 crisis
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Tumbling technology-related shares led a global stock sell off on Friday, with US traders searching for safe havens as the US 10-year yield dropped by the most in a month.
Traders ‌sold stocks in most markets with Japan and Korea down more than 5% overnight. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, ‌their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while on Wall Street chip-maker shares fell 10.7% Friday and 17.1% for the week.
Anthropic, which debuted this week, fell as much as ​14.5% on its first full day of trading, just above its $83 IPO pricing, and ended down 9.1% at $88.30.
Consumer staples was the sole S&P 500 sector to end in the black on Friday.
"Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.
"Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the ‌outlook for corporate profitability."
The Dow Jones Industrial ⁠Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe ⁠fell 34.89 points, or 3.30%, to 1,021.91. Its weekly decline of 8.1% was the largest since early 2020.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 2%, emerging market stocks fell 3.10% and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed lower by 3.27%. Japan's Nikkei fell 5.06%.
The VIX index, linked to ​the cost ​of insurance against a drop in the S&P 500, closed at its highest ​since April 2025.
As investors sought safe-haven assets, government bonds ‌rallied.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 10.43 basis points to 4.948%, the largest daily drop since October 22. The 30-year bond yield fell 6.81 basis points to 5.3329%. The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, fell 13.21 basis points to 4.647% even as a rate hike is priced in for next month's policy meeting.
DOLLAR FLAT, OIL RISES LATE
The dollar index was little changed after touching a 19-month high on Thursday. The dollar's recent rally has been fueled by bets on ‌tighter monetary policy due to hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
"I think the momentum ​has stalled for the dollar ... but I think it's a little bit early to ​pick a top for the dollar," said Marc Chandler, ​chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.
The dollar index fell 0.05% to 103.90, with the euro down ‌0.05% at $1.0961. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar weakened 0.67% ​to 158.6.
In commodities, crude prices ​rose late on Friday on worries about possible attacks in the US-Israeli war with Iran, and as traders bought crude ahead of next week's Thanksgiving holiday.
US crude rose 1.49% to $83.67 a barrel and Brent rose to $92.61 per barrel, up 0.68% on the ​day.
Gold prices fell to a 14-month low ‌after the largest weekly drop in 8 months.
Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.09 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.22% ​to $40.95 an ounce. Copper declined 2.9% to $12,162.50 a ton.
(Reporting by Rodrigo Campos, Harry Robertson, Anna Hirtenstein, Saqib Iqbal Ahmed; ​editing by Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Nick Zieminski and Jonathan Spicer )

articles.title_orig: Anthropic stock drops 8% after rip-roaring IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic stock drops 8% after rip-roaring IPO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Call it the Anthropic ( ANT ) IPO hangover.
Shares of the model builder dropped nearly 8.5% on Friday as investors booked profits after a frenetic first day of trading. Not helping sentiment: The broader market plunged on Anthropic's well-received IPO day and remains under pressure today.
Follow live updates amid Friday's worst sell-off since 2025.
Anthropic made a monster debut on Wall Street Thursday, with shares opening at $111.50 a little before noon ET, a 34% premium to the $83 IPO price.
But the AI company's stock couldn't hold on to its early gains.
The stock closed at $97.17, up 17% on the day. That closing price gave Anthropic a market capitalization of about $1.28 trillion, or roughly $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Not bad for a company founded only five years ago, in a historic IPO that raised $81.3 billion.
On Friday, the stock closed just below $89 per share with a market cap of $1.17 trillion.
"At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic's debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives said.

articles.title_orig: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.title_zh: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.content_orig:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.
The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.
Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.
Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.
The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.
The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices , rising interest rates , mounting corporate debt loads , stubborn inflation , supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.
“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”
Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome.
Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said.
“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock extends $2.5 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.
The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.
Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.
"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.title_zh: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.content_orig:
Chief of staff Stephen Miller praises President Trump's record on deregulation and the economy, and Trump jokingly asks if he wants to run for president.
During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by.
The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing.
Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028
President Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio look on during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Trump addressed the media after returning from a visit to China where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office.
"I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said.
He then rattled some of them off, including:
White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller speaks during a press briefing at the White House, Thursday, May 1, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
"Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader."
Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans.
"We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference.
"Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group.
STEPHEN MILLER'S INTERNAL MEMO UNLEASHES TRUMP AGENCIES AFTER 'ABSOLUTE CONTROL' UNDER WILES' REIGN
Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. Trump vowed to tax American companies that build data centers in other countries, though he did not detail how such a threat would be carried out or what legal authority the government might have to impose one. (Yuri Gripas/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028 . But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring.
Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans.

Miller's name has not been previously floated as a contender for launching a White House bid.

articles.title_orig: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.title_zh: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.title_zh: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_zh: Trump considering new Iran strikes as US military warns of strain on forces
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile Friday, causing a fire onboard the vessel but no injuries, according to a British naval monitor.
The tanker was traveling out of the key waterway when it was struck by an unknown projectile, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.
The UKMTO earlier reported that a bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, had reported shots being fired in its vicinity by assailants on a small boat.
During Friday's news conference, President Trump said that during his trilateral with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping, the three leaders discussed nuclear responsibilities.
Mr. Trump said they "spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet" and that "in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
As he lauded slightly lower gas prices during a news conference at the White House on Friday, President Trump said the U.S. wants a "real deal" with Iran, not a "fake" deal.
"They want to make a deal but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," he said.
"They've been bulls******g people for 51 years," the president said of Iran.
U.S. Central Command denied carrying out any new strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island on Friday after Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is closely linked with the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said a missile had hit the island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tasnim said it had no information of any possible damage, and other Iranian media outlets offered more vague details. The semi-official Fars news agency said an explosion was heard in the skies over the island, but that the cause was unknown.
The U.S. has attacked the island several times, most recently on Tuesday with what a military official described to CBS News as precision strikes on an IRGC missile site.
The official said that strike was launched "in self-defense … in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Friday that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's government in the impoverished nation's more than decade-long civil war against the Iran-backed rebel group.
The latest missiles launched by the Houthis targeted the Jazan region, on the southwest Saudi coast near the border with Yemen, but "air defense intercepted and destroyed" them, according to coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki.
The Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district earlier this week.
A bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, has reported shots being fired in its vicinity by armed men on a small boat, according to a British naval monitor.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, which is run by the British navy, said Friday that the ship was traveling eastbound when it was approached "by a dark blue skiff with six unidentified, armed persons on board."
"Four shots were fired in quick succession from the skiff and warning shots were returned by the armed security team onboard the bulk carrier," UKTMO said, adding that there was no damage reported to the vessel or its crew.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district Friday as the group issued a series of threats against Saudi Arabia.
"We announce that (King Abdullah Financial District) in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, is a military target for our forces. We therefore call on all employees, workers and citizens to stay away from it immediately," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
In a Telegram post Friday, Saree wrote: "We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries. Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of damaging a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district with a strike earlier this week.
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions .
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.
The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.
For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in the escalating conflict with Iran's Houthi allies warned civilians Friday to leave the area around the key port

articles.title_orig: The Nasdaq Just Had Its 6th Correction in 4 Years. History Says This Is the Likelihood of a Full-Blown Bear Market
articles.title_zh: The Nasdaq Just Had Its 6th Correction in 4 Years. History Says This Is the Likelihood of a Full-Blown Bear Market
articles.content_orig:
By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:57PM EST
10 stocks we like better than NASDAQ Composite Index ›
Tech stocks are having a brutal November. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -5.28% ) is now down nearly 17% from its Oct. 6 peak. A correction means an index closes at least 10% below its record, while a bear market means a decline of 20% or more.
Several factors are weighing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, including disappointing earnings from hyperscalers and a Blue Tsunami in the midterm elections that raised concerns about further regulations and restrictions on data centers .
Add in the Jensen Huang scandal and a Federal Reserve leaning toward more interest rate hikes, and investors have plenty to worry about. This is the Nasdaq's sixth correction in four years, which have overall been quite prosperous for investors.
History suggests these are the odds that the correction will turn into a full-blown bear market.
Image source: Getty Images.
As I mentioned, while the stock market has had a terrific four years, it has been volatile and also had its fair share of ups and downs, including five corrections prior to the current one.
As you can see, corrections are more common than one might suspect. In fact, a 2024 Reuters study of LSEG data found that the Nasdaq has experienced 24 corrections over the past 44 years. According to Dow Jones Market Data, the Nasdaq has extended a correction into a bear market about 37% of the time since 1971.
The good news is that the majority of corrections tend to revert back higher. The bad news is that there is still a decent chance that a correction could morph into a full-blown bear market , and the Nasdaq is not far from one as of this writing.
This is the reality for Nasdaq investors. Investing more heavily in tech can yield fantastic gains, but typically entails greater turbulence. History also tells us the Nasdaq has generated fantastic gains. Since the turn of the century, the Nasdaq has generated a total return of 467%, besting the broader benchmark S&P 500's total return of nearly 379%.
This includes the Dot-Com Bubble, in which the Nasdaq lost roughly 77% of its value between 2000 and 2002. So, long-term investors can stay invested in the Nasdaq, but it really depends on your risk tolerance. If you can't handle big swings multiple times a year, then the Nasdaq might not be the right index for you.

articles.title_orig: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.title_zh: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: 10 years on, Britain reopens the Brexit fight — this time embracing the E.U.
articles.title_zh: 10 years on, Britain reopens the Brexit fight — this time embracing the E.U.
articles.content_orig:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK
The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.
Burnham ‌said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029 , but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year ‌with the EU about what could be achieved next.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, ‌the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.

Britain ⁠prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.

The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.

The UK prime minister called the newly agreed post-Brexit reset deal a “win-win” for the UK and the EU, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
The prime minister met Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at the EU-UK summit in Brussels.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed that Andy Burnham’s reset agreements with the EU “was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024”.
He also said Burnham’s actions “went completely against the pledge that he made to the voters of Makerfield just a few months ago”.
The Reform leader later added: “Burnham’s whole rationale is 73% of the people want to be closer to Europe .
“Well, if you ask me do I want better relations with our European neighbours? Do I think we could have a better trade deal than we’ve got at the moment? I am part of that 73%.
“But what he completely misunderstands is that is not an open ticket to rejoin a significant chunk of the single market today.”

Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.
It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.
An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.

After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests , governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.

articles.title_orig: Trump defends Putin ties and accuses Iran of bad faith
articles.title_zh: Trump defends Putin ties and accuses Iran of bad faith
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.
On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.
“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.
Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”. He said there was “great electricity” between the leaders of the world’s main nuclear powers.
“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.
“I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that,” he also said.
No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.
The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.
Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war , which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.
“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”
Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”
During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.
Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”
“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”
Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.
“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”
Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.
“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”
Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

articles.title_zh: FDA urgently recalls sandwiches over dangerous ‘organism’ linked to fatal infections
articles.content_orig:
The US Food and Drug Administration has recalled a line of grab-and-go breakfast sandwiches over fears they’re contaminated with a terrifying organism linked to fatal infections, stillbirths, and miscarriages.
Grand Strand Sandwich Company Inc. asked to rip the items from shelves on Thursday after discovering the dangerous contaminant.
Its Lunch Box-branded sandwiches, which were sold in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Virginia, potentially contain Listeria monocytogenes, an organism which can cause the serious infection listeriosis, the FDA announced.
The affected products were distributed between March 2 and Nov. 10 and include:
The sandwiches were sold at convenience stores, vending machines and prison canteens. No illnesses have been linked to the items.
Those with weaker immune systems who contract the bug like young children, elderly people, and pregnant women could face short-term symptoms like high fever, severe headaches, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Pregnant women could also suffer miscarriages, stillbirths, premature delivery or life-threatening infection of the newborn if the nasty organism infects the fetus.
Anyone who has purchased a recalled item is urged to throw the item away immediately, especially if it could be hiding in the back of a freezer or pantry.
Affected products can be redeemed for a refund if the packaging is brought to the retailer where it was bought.
Shoppers with questions about the recall can contact Grand Strand Sandwich at 843-399-2999 from Monday to Thursday between the hours of 8 p.m. and 4 p.m. and on Friday between 8 a.m. and 12 p.m.
This latest recall came just days after 2,414 other breakfast sandwiches were also recalled over listeria fears.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
The drama over AI in the math community is getting real.
Hours after Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said he solved the most famous open problem in the field using AI on Friday, another mathematician came out of the woodwork to announce he'd also solved the problem.
Only this mathematician said he did it without using AI.
Alessandro Masullo, a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford, said he's been working on the problem for 12 years and was about a year away from releasing his results when he was blindsided by Alpöge's report.
"In light of the current climate I am being advised to release the current version as it is," he said in a paper posted online, adding that there may be errors in it because it was rushed.
And in a thinly veiled slight against Alpöge, who described working with Claude for weeks to reach his solution, Masullo said that human mathematicians still have a place in the age of AI.
"If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here," he said. "We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere."
Masullo's solution, which is far shorter than Alpöge's, immediately sparked a further firestorm in a math community already reeling from the unprecedented Anthropic paper and months of AI companies announcing high-profile solutions to long-standing math problems.
"The plot thickens!" Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell, said on X on Friday.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Now it's getting more complicated," Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech , told Business Insider.
Mathematicians are now racing to scrutinize both solutions with their own brains and with AI. Neither had, by Friday afternoon, been formally proven.
At stake is nothing less than the credibility of human mathematicians in the age of AI, and who's solution is right will have grave implications for the future of mathematics.
Masullo, his partner at Stanford, Brian Conrad, and Alpöge did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.
The problem in question is the Riemann Hypothesis, which Strogatz described to Business Insider as the "White Whale" of mathematics. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers.
The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician $1 million. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category.
Gukov, the math professor at Caltech, called the claim that it was solved a "HUGE deal."
"RH was the biggest problem in math," he said, using the past tense.

articles.title_zh: Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Following the Android deprecation in September, Google Assistant is going away on speakers and smart displays next year. Additionally, Google Home is fully replacing the Nest app in January.
The Nest app on Android, iOS, and the web will stop working on January 25, 2027. The Google Home app, which requires a Google Account, will be needed to “continue controlling and receiving notifications from your Nest devices remotely.”
Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:
With home.nest.com going away, you have to download any custom video clips since they will not transfer over to Google Home. A one-click “Download All” button is available.
Terrible news. For all my first-gen Nest cameras (wired hello doorbell, wired outdoor cams, and multiple indoor cams), I vastly prefer the Nest app to the terrible Google Home app.
Otherwise, Nest app users do not need to do anything else, with devices automatically transferring over to the Google Home app. No Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke alarms, or locks are losing support with this change.
Additionally, Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions will automatically switch to Google Home Premium “with no additional cost and no credit card re-entry required at this time.”
The other change announced today is that Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays is going away on August 2, 2027. It will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant. Google notes that natural language support replaces “rigid, static and highly specific voice commands.” Additionally:
You can upgrade to Gemini today , while Google is expanding international availability over the coming months. Google will share more updates closer to the deadline.
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
